text: Hello everyone. We are presenting Sentinel, an AI powered citizen incident reporting and intelligent emergency dispatch system. It was developed by Latheshkumar, Madesh, Jeffrin and Kamalesh Balaji, under the guidance of Ms. Sumitha T, for the Product Development Lab at R.M.K. Engineering College.

Today, when a citizen in Chennai sees a fire, an accident or a flooded road, the only option is to call a helpline and describe it. A phone call carries no photo or video. The location is a vague landmark. One visible incident triggers dozens of duplicate calls. And calls are handled in the order they arrive, not by how serious they are.

Sentinel fixes this in three steps. Citizens report with evidence and an exact GPS location. An AI pipeline verifies, summarises, de-duplicates and prioritises every report. And dispatchers see a live map and send the nearest responder in one click.

The system has four tiers. A React progressive web app for citizens and dispatchers. A FastAPI backend with secure login and live WebSocket updates. PostgreSQL and Redis for data. And an AI worker that runs every report through the pipeline.

The pipeline runs YOLO version 8 on photos and video frames, checks the photo's EXIF data against the reported location, and transcribes voice notes with Whisper. A Qwen 3.5 language model, running locally through llama dot c p p, extracts the hazard type, severity and a summary. Sentence embeddings and a Union Find algorithm merge duplicate reports, and a weighted score sets the priority. If any model is missing, Sentinel records that honestly instead of guessing.

Let us see it working. A citizen opens Sentinel on their phone, chooses Road Accident, and describes what they see at Kathipara junction. They attach a photo, and tap Use my location to fill in the exact GPS coordinates. One tap submits the report.
The report is saved instantly and the citizen receives a tracking ID. In the background, the AI pipeline has already started working on it.
With the tracking ID, the citizen can follow the report through seven stages, from Reported, through AI Processing and Verified, all the way to Closed.

Now the dispatcher signs in. The dashboard shows every active incident across Chennai, from Ennore in the north to Tambaram in the south. The cards at the top show incidents by severity, available units, and duplicate clusters. The heat map highlights where incidents are concentrated, and the live feed on the right is sorted by priority.

Here is the report we just submitted. YOLO detected the bus and the people in the photo, and the language model turned the citizen's words into a structured record: a road accident at Kathipara junction, needing an immediate response, with a one line summary. The provenance block shows exactly which models ran.

This transformer fire on Ranganathan Street in T. Nagar was reported three times by different people. Sentinel merged the reports into one cluster, which raised its priority. The k d tree lists the nearest available responders with their distance. Officer Priya Nair from Fire and Rescue is only a hundred and fifty metres away, so the dispatcher sends her with one click, and the status moves to Dispatched.

The analytics page shows the category and status breakdown, available units, duplicate clusters, and the average time to dispatch and to resolve, so the control room can measure and improve its response.

On our Chennai dataset of eighteen reports, all three duplicate groups were merged correctly, and each report was triaged in about seven seconds on a single laptop GPU. The project has one hundred and eleven automated tests, and all of them pass.
In the future, Sentinel can be connected to the 112 emergency response system, support Tamil and other languages, and add a responder mobile app and flood hotspot prediction for the monsoon.
